newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Labour win to change workers laws in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Labour win to change workers laws in Britain.

text.p: British workers can expect the same level of social protection as their continental cousins if Britain's new Labour government keeps its promise to sign the European Union's Social Chapter.

By signing up, Britain would agree to take on board the two EU directives already adopted under the Social Chapter -- a law which gives new parents three months unpaid leave and another that obliges multinational firms with more than 1,000 employees to have procedures for consulting their workers.

It would also enable British ministers to take part in EU talks on two further proposals for social legislation -- an agreement to improve the rights of part-time workers and a directive shifting more of the burden of proof in sex discrimination cases on to the employer.

Under the opt-out negotiated by Britain's outgoing Conservative government, Britain, unlike its 14 EU partners, is not bound by the minimum working conditions set by the Social Chapter and plays no part in EU ministerial negotiations on proposals for future laws.

If the Tony Blair government signs up, Britain will have to apply the rules like everyone else, an EU official told Reuters, but he was optimistic this would not pose major difficulties, especially as many British-based firms had already decided voluntarily to comply with the Works Council directive.

A British diplomat in Brussels said the change would have implications for other EU countries too, as continental firms with employees in Britain could find they were over the 1,000- worker threshold and be obliged to set up worker consultation.
The new Labour government would probably ask for a grace period to bring in existing European laws, just as Austria, Finland and Sweden did when they joined the EU in 1995, he said.

EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said on Friday he hoped EU leaders, who meet next month in Amsterdam, would agree to change the EU's Maastricht Treaty so that the Social Chapter applied to all 15 EU states.
"I believe...that there should be a common base for social rights for all the people in the European Union," the Irish commissioner said in a statement.

Ratifying any changes to the treaty is expected to take the Union's 15 national parliaments at least two years but the British diplomat said Labour would probably try to introduce the European social laws before then.
The British Chamber of Commerce on Friday urged Blair to keep Britain out of the Social Chapter "in order to protect labour market flexibility".
But Bill Morris, leader of Britain's largest trade union, told the BBC the Social Chapter was "a framework for decency".
If and when Britain does sign up to the Social Chapter, London will still retain a veto over a number of EU social policy decisions.

It only needs a qualified majority of EU states to get in the statute books Social Chapter laws on workers' health and safety, working conditions, sexual equality at work and the right of employees to be consulted by management.
But Britain, like any other EU country, would still have the right to block decisions on other important aspects of industrial relations which need unanimous approval to come into force.
These include laws on social security, trade union membership, the right to strike and levels of pay.
